overview:
The state took its name from a people who no longer existed as such: the Baltic-speaking Prussians of the southeastern Baltic coast, conquered and largely absorbed by the Teutonic Knights over the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. What began in 1525 was the Order's own dissolution. Its last grand master, Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach, took Luther's advice, secularised the Order's lands, and by the Treaty of Kraków received them back as a hereditary duchy held in fief from the Polish crown, kneeling before Sigismund I in Kraków's market square that April. Ducal Prussia became the first state in Europe to adopt Lutheranism as its established church, and Albert's university at Königsberg, founded in 1544, turned out clergy and printed books in Lithuanian and Polish as well as German. The duchy passed by inheritance to the Hohenzollern electors of Brandenburg in 1618, joining two scattered territories that did not touch each other. Frederick William, the Great Elector, shook off Polish overlordship at Wehlau in 1657 and Oliva in 1660, and spent the rest of his reign building the standing army and centralised bureaucracy that later observers would treat as Prussia's essential character.

His grandson crowned himself King in Prussia at Königsberg in 1701 — the title had to be worded carefully, since Brandenburg still lay inside the Holy Roman Empire. The eighteenth century made the kingdom a great power on thin material foundations: Frederick William I drilled the army and the tax administration, and Frederick II seized Silesia from Austria in 1740, held it through the near-catastrophe of the Seven Years' War, and shared in the partitions that erased Poland from the map. Collapse came fast at Jena and Auerstedt in 1806, and the humiliation produced the Stein–Hardenberg reforms, the emancipation of the serfs, Scharnhorst's remade army and Humboldt's university in Berlin. Restored and enlarged at Vienna in 1815 with the Rhineland and Westphalia, Prussia acquired the coal and iron that would make it Germany's industrial core, and through the Zollverein it bound the other German states to its economy before it bound them to its politics. Bismarck's wars against Denmark, Austria and France between 1864 and 1871 ended with the Prussian king proclaimed German emperor at Versailles. Prussia then occupied an odd position: it held roughly two-thirds of the new empire's territory and people, yet its own parliament was elected on a three-class franchise weighted heavily toward wealth. After 1918 the paradox reversed. The Free State of Prussia became one of the Weimar Republic's steadiest democracies, governed for most of the 1920s by the Social Democrat Otto Braun, until Franz von Papen removed that government by presidential decree on 20 July 1932 — the Preussenschlag — and handed the largest German state, and its police, to the Reich. Hermann Göring took it over months later. The Allied Control Council formally abolished Prussia on 25 February 1947, declaring that a state "which from early days has been a bearer of militarism and reaction in Germany has de facto ceased to exist."
significance: Prussia is the state that made modern Germany, and the argument over whether it also made German catastrophe has never fully settled. Its administrative model — a professional civil service, universal conscription, compulsory schooling, a reformed university, codified law — was studied and copied from Japan to Chile, and much of what the nineteenth century meant by an efficient state was learned by watching Berlin. The same institutions carried a political legacy that outlasted the monarchy: a landed officer class with disproportionate weight, a habit of governing by administration rather than assembly, and a franchise designed to keep an industrial society under pre-industrial control. The Allies' 1947 verdict, that Prussia had been a bearer of militarism and reaction, wrote a particular reading of that history into law and dissolved the state that had defined central Europe for two and a half centuries, redistributing its lands among new German Länder and, east of the Oder, among Poland and the Soviet Union.
coverage: The dataset holds no events at all beneath this story, so everything here is drawn from general reference works rather than from the map's own material; nothing above can be placed or dated on the timeline. Two things are genuinely thin in the underlying record as well: the Old Prussians themselves, whose language and religion survive mainly through the writings of the crusading Order that destroyed them, and the interpretive question of whether the Prussian state naturally led to 1933 — a claim the 1947 abolition law asserts flatly and that historians have argued over ever since, with the Weimar Free State's democratic record cutting hard against it.
